Date: 2026-11-09

summary: Walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript), auth patterns, environment setup and quickstarts. Discussed hosted vs Dedicated, VPC/on-prem options, KMS, and next steps for pilot and pricing.
topics: Auth: API keys vs SSO/service accounts/KMS
Environment / env vars and local dev
Console walkthrough for routes and batching settings
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, this is Sofia our SE, and today we're gonna run through the SDK quickstarts for Python and TypeScript, auth, env setup and a quick console demo.
[00:12] Michael: Great, thanks. We're mainly looking to get something in prod by Q1, current stack is Node + Python services, Kubernetes on AWS, and we care a lot about latency and data residency.
[00:25] Sofia: Awesome, that helps. Quick question, Samir, any VPC or egress constraints we should know about up front?
[00:31] Samir: Yeah, we have strict egress rules, need to go through our proxy and all outbound must be via our NAT. We also need to ensure any keys are stored in our KMS, so we can't embed secrets in images.
[00:42] Sofia: Understood, Redwood Private supports VPC peering and we also have options for on-prem packages, plus KMS/HSM integrations. We'll share the exact network requirements doc after.
[00:51] Rebecca: For the SDKs, we want examples in both Python and TypeScript — minimal setup for devs to run locally and then containerize.
[00:58] Jordan: Yep. Sofia, do you want to jump into the SDK demo?
[01:03] Sofia: Sure. I'll share my screen — quick caveat, screen share may show some prod-ish config names, ignore those — here's the PyPI package, pip install redwood-inference (note: transcript may read as redwood inference or redwood-inf, audio messed this up earlier).
[01:18] Sofia: Basic Python quickstart: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, then from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); response = client.generate('Summarize customer message') — simple. For TS: npm i @redwood/inference, then import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood(process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY); const out = await client.generate(...).
[01:42] Michael: Are there built-in retries and timeouts? We have strict SLOs.
[01:48] Sofia: SDK has configurable timeouts, retries, and streaming. We recommend timeout of 3-5s for low-latency endpoints and a separate background worker for long-running generations. Also we offer client-side batching helpers if you want to merge small requests.
[02:05] Rebecca: How about auth for service accounts — we don't want to use a single API key for everything.
[02:10] Jordan: Good point. We support scoped API keys, short-lived tokens via our control plane, and full SSO with role mapping for console access. For service-to-service use, use a service account key stored in your KMS and rotate it via CI.
[02:25] Samir: Rotation workflow — can we integrate with AWS KMS and IAM roles?
[02:30] Sofia: Yes, we have examples for AWS KMS and you can use our token exchange flow: your infra asks Redwood for a short-lived token using mutual TLS or a signed JWT. We'll share the sample repo.
[02:42] Michael: On deployment modes — hosted API vs Dedicated — what's the tradeoff re latency/cost?
[02:48] Jordan: Hosted is fastest to onboard, pay-as-you-go and we have tuned open-models with predictable perf; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, lower unit cost at scale, and tighter isolation. For latency-critical workloads we tend to recommend Dedicated with pinned model variants, but if you're just validating, start hosted.
[03:07] Rebecca: For Dedicated, how much lead time for provisioning?
[03:10] Jordan: Usually a couple of weeks depending on region and capacity; for pilots we can carve out burst capacity sooner.
[03:16] Sofia: On the console side, quick tour — routes, per-route model pins, batching and cache settings. If you head to the Console -> Routes, set model to gptx-8k-qat (note: audio turned that into g-p-t-x, transcript may be off) and set max tokens, batching window. The Optimize tab will give suggestions based on your traffic like enabling prefix caching or recommending a quantized model.
[03:42] Michael: Can Optimize suggest quantization profiles? We run lots of short chat interactions.
[03:46] Sofia: Yes, Optimize will recommend quantization and batching settings based on latency and unit-cost tradeoffs and you can simulate expected token costs. We'll export a sample report.
[03:58] Rebecca: Any limitations with streaming or webhooks?
[04:02] Sofia: Streaming is supported in both SDKs and we've got examples for Node server-sent events. Webhooks for async jobs are supported too, with retry semantics.
[04:12] Michael: Ok good. Let's go back to the quickstarts — what's the minimal env setup for a dev?
[04:18] Sofia: For local dev: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your shell, optionally set REDWOOD_API_URL if you want to target a staging endpoint, and REDWOOD_ENV=local. We have a docker-compose quickstart that runs a mock server for offline dev. We'll add that link.
[04:33] Jordan: Also, for CI/CD we recommend storing keys in KMS and pulling them at build time or using an identity provider to mint short-lived tokens.
[04:41] Samir: About network egress — if we need to route through a proxy, is there SDK support for proxy env vars?
[04:47] Sofia: Yes, both SDKs respect standard HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY env vars, and we have instructions for setting up VPC peering + private endpoints for Redwood Private.
[04:56] Rebecca: Are audit logs available per token? We need traceability for compliance.
[05:00] Jordan: Audit logs are available; we can show you the retention settings in the Console and we also provide export hooks to your SIEM.
[05:06] Michael: SOC 2 and ISO?
[05:09] Jordan: We are SOC 2 compliant and can provide the summary plus the full attestation under NDA. We'll attach that.
[05:16] Rebecca: For the pilot, we want a small benchmark — 100 concurrent chat sessions, avg 150 tokens per response. Can we run that?
[05:23] Sofia: Yes, we can run a benchmark on hosted or Dedicated. For accurate results we prefer you to run a replay from your traffic or let us run a synthetic benchmark simulating your latency distribution.
[05:33] Michael: Any gotchas with kv-cache or long-context? We use some retrieval for customers.
[05:37] Sofia: KV cache is mostly internal in the runtime, and for retrieval we recommend chunking and using embeddings service; Optimize can recommend cache TTLs. For very long contexts, pin a model variant optimized for long sequences — Console shows model profiles.
[05:50] Rebecca: About SDK versions and pinning — we want reproducible behavior between dev and prod.
[05:55] Jordan: Pin the SDK version in package.json/requirements, and on the server side pin the model version in the Console's route config. We also offer canary rollouts for model changes.
[06:07] Samir: Logging — we need token-level cost breakdowns for chargeback.
[06:11] Sofia: That's in the Console Usage tab, and you can export token-level logs via API. We'll include a sample export.
[06:20] [09:30] Sofia: (later in demo) quick sample TS snippet showing streaming with EventSource, note: small glitches in audio may show as redwoood or redwoodd on transcript.
[07:05] Michael: When you say "prefix caching" can you explain simply?
[07:08] Sofia: Sure — prefix or KV caching saves repeated parts of the prompt/latents so you don't recompute the same tokens; it's most helpful if you have repeated system messages or templates.
[07:20] Rebecca: Is there client side instrumentation to help us measure batching efficiency?
[07:24] Sofia: Yes, SDK provides hooks to report request size and latency so you can compute effective batching. The Optimize console also surfaces batch sizes and recommends target batch windows.
[07:35] Jordan: Quick note about cost — we can show modeled unit costs for a given qps and average token length; we'll include a quick calculator in the follow up.
[07:45] Samir: Security question — do we ever store customer data? We need to ensure data residency and retention rules.
[07:51] Jordan: For Hosted, we do retain logs for X days by default but you can opt out; Dedicated/Private gives you full control and no shared storage. We'll share the retention policy doc.
[08:05] Rebecca: For the sample quickstart repo, can you include a Dockerfile and GitHub action that pulls secret from KMS?
[08:11] Sofia: Absolutely, sample CI/CD snippets will be in the repo link we'll share.
[08:18] Michael: About SDK licensing and usage limits — do we get rate limits per key?
[08:23] Jordan: Hosted has rate limits and quotas per-key; with Dedicated you can configure throughput and autoscaling. For pilots we set temporary higher quotas.
[08:33] Rebecca: Can we get a sandbox account with elevated quota for the benchmark?
[08:36] Jordan: Yes, we'll provision a sandbox for the pilot week of Nov 16.
[08:40] [15:00] Sofia: Quick note on error codes — SDK surfaces 429 with retry-after, 503 for infra; we recommend exponential backoff.
[08:52] Michael: Any differences in SDK behavior for function/tool calling vs plain text generation?
[08:57] Sofia: We have structured output helpers and function-calling patterns; the TS SDK offers typed interfaces to define tool schemas.
[09:06] Rebecca: Great. I think that covers technical questions.
[09:10] Jordan: Recap: we'll send the SDK quickstart repo, security docs (SOC2 + KMS integration), sample Docker + CI snippets, and a pricing/proposal for Dedicated options. We'll also provision a sandbox for the pilot the week of 2026-11-16.
[09:25] Michael: Perfect.
[09:28] Jordan: Any last minute items?
[09:30] Samir: I'll upload our infra diagram and firewall rules to the shared folder by Friday.
[09:33] Jordan: Great, action items noted. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with links.
[09:40] Rebecca: Thanks all.
[09:42] Jordan: End.
[42:00] (call ends)
